sentences.text: The Bossware and Employment Tech Database is a database (Labor Vector census record) of which its operator writes, "Coworker.org’s Bossware and Employment Tech database compiles more than 550 labor-focused technology products that are changing our relationship to work" (Coworker, database page), counted by the census as 635 product rows in the page saved on 2026-10-29 (census record), and its report gives the same products as "assembled into a searchable database and dubbed Little Tech" (the report).

The page is dated 17 November 2021 (Coworker, database page); the research ran from November 2020 to May 2021 and catalogued products, "not the companies that created" them, 31% of which emerged between 2020 and 2021 and the rest between 2018 and 2020 (the report), the period the census records (census record).

Its operator places it in a trend, "Since 2018 we’ve seen a rise in the use of tech to manage the world’s labor force", and gives its scope as companies, "and their products and investors", that "touch every part of the labor process, from hiring to productivity monitoring and more", products "that use technology like AI, location tracking, and biometrics to manage employees and collect their data — often without their knowledge", the table being there to "learn more about the companies behind this emerging trend" (Coworker, database page).

The census reads it first under AI governing labor, "hiring, surveillance, scheduling, quotas, evaluation and discipline", then under the distribution of gains and losses and under worker power (census record), and puts to it its organizing question, "Who supplies the labor, who directs it, and who receives its gains" (census record).

The record answers from the table itself: the labor is supplied by the workers each product targets, hourly, contract, salaried, non-management and management, the report centring low-wage and hourly workers; it is directed by "employers who buy and deploy the products", through the vendors who make them; and the gains go to the vendors and investors each row names (census record), while the report states that the products are contributing to the reduction of labor standards, continuing to shift the costs of production onto workers, and fissuring labor markets (the report).

Its unit is one table row per product, with the parent company, category, type, targeted workers, investors and assessments of its data practices against worker-rights criteria, and its evidence is of two kinds, a product inventory and a rating against standards (census record).

The report sorts the products into four areas, performance and productivity monitoring, safety, benefits, health and well-being, and labor, job market and workplace optimization, and finds most of them promoting workplace safety (40%) or optimizing the functioning of labor markets (38%) (the report).

The census's tally of the saved table gives 242 rows in Labor Market Optimization, 178 in performance and productivity monitoring, 176 in safety, 34 in benefits and 5 in two categories, 595 products in use and 206 emerged during Covid-19, and it records as unchecked that the report's 40% and 38% are not reproduced by the table and whether the rows include products added after the report (census record); the table opens row by row on the page (Coworker, database page), with the report as a PDF download (census record).

Each row assesses the product's own terms against worker-rights criteria, among them "Informed consent obtained", whether the worker can access, interpret and correct their own data, a grievance mechanism, forced use of the tool, discrimination potential and the right to freedom of association (Coworker, database page), an analysis the report says had to move "beyond a privacy-only framework", and on privacy itself it finds that "Only 35% of the products share any information on privacy policy and data sharing arrangements" (the report).

The accompanying report, Little Tech Is Coming for Workers: A Framework for Reclaiming and Building Worker Power, by Wilneida Negrón, PhD, "analyzes the ways they’re harming workers, labor standards, and the economy" (Coworker, database page); it is © 2021 Coworker.org under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (the report), the licence the census records for the report alone, none being stated for the table (census record).

The report names the marketplace the database catalogues Little Tech, the unregulated marketplace of tech products, companies and investors collecting and aggregating data about workers at almost every step of the labor process, and credits the database's research and making to Ayden Federline (the report).

Its first finding is that "The current proliferation of tech products has the potential to continue eroding labor standards and weaken worker voice and worker power, while also increasing the potential for discrimination and other harms", among the ways it names the accelerating commodification of low-wage workers' data (the report).

It finds a historic amount of private capital behind the products' proliferation and low-wage workers navigating "scientifically questionable" hiring and background check technologies, and its conclusion explores the implications of more than 550 products that appeared in the workplace and job markets during the pandemic (the report).

Hiring is in the table as products: the HireVue row, "HireVue AI Facial Recognition", under Labor Market Optimization, describes video interviews and AI-driven pre-hire assessments in which job seekers' behavior, intonation and speech are fed to an algorithm that assigns traits, and records the product as Discontinued (Coworker, database page).

Of that class the archive's measure of uncompensated applicant labor applies, by its own statement of scope, to technical hiring platforms and "AI interview firms" (#747), and AI interview platforms, "Firms like HireVue, Karat, and emerging AI-mediated interview operators", collect video, audio, response timing and behavioral data from candidates at scale, data that is institutional capital while "The candidates' labor is supplied free" (#747).

What a screening apparatus produces, on #747's definition, is calibration intelligence, durable knowledge derived from aggregate applicant interaction and "the operator's principal source of competitive advantage"; technical-hiring platforms capture calibration data while candidates pay in unpaid preparation labor, and rejected applicants become the training set of the next cycle's apparatus (#747).

#747 states its own limit, alleging no individual design, no illegality and no uniquely culpable party, "Structural extraction does not require an extractor", and asks only "that the relation be named correctly" (#747).

The report states that the database "is not exhaustive", hundreds more emerging products and non-U.S. products having been omitted or overlooked, and that collection stopped once the researchers felt they had sufficient evidence of Little Tech's pervasiveness; built at the product level, it omits smaller Big Tech companies, Uber, Lyft and DoorDash among them (the report).

Its method is desk research on public documents, investors from Crunchbase, app permissions from the Google Play store and privacy from public privacy statements, terms of service and impact assessments (the report; census record); the report primarily discusses low-wage and hourly workers, and holds that workers' own reports would show how the technologies are implemented in the workplace beyond the products' stated uses and business goals (the report).

The census carries the limits as its coverage, 42 origin territories with 461 of 635 rows from the United States, non-U.S. products omitted or overlooked, as a stated limit, and as two negative tags, "NOT an exhaustive census of workplace technology" and "NOT a record of the Big Tech gig platforms, which it omits" (census record).

Its lifecycle is historical, with no later update stated on the saved page, and the census tags it "NOT a measure of how widely any product is deployed" and "NOT updated since 2021 on the saved page"; its evidence can settle which workplace technology products existed in 2020 to 2021 and what their public documents say about consent, access to data, grievance, data sharing and law-enforcement access, and cannot settle how any product is used at a workplace or how often, its effect on wages, workload or employment, or products after May 2021 (census record).

The page invites workers to share their stories (Coworker, database page), and the report holds that listing, classifying and analyzing Little Tech's direct harms can build worker voice and power and strengthen regulation (the report); the census tags the database "NOT worker testimony", the table holding none (census record).

In the archive's reading the database "inventories the products through which employers direct work and collect workers' data, product by product" and "meets the directionality stack at the layer of who directs labor"; it records nothing on whether a system's labor advanced a commissioned task, "so DSL and task-origin find no measurement in it" (census record).

Its operator is Coworker.org, "a global platform to advance change in the workplace" (Coworker, database page); the report compares its data points with the "UC Berkeley Labor Center’s list in their report" (the report), and the census makes Negotiating Tech its neighbour (census record).

Bossware, the word in its name, is given in the press as "technology and AI tools used by managers to supervise, surveil, and track employee habits, output, and biometrics" (New York Times, snippet only), and in video titles as watching people while they work (Bloomberg Originals), as "70% of U.S. Employers Track Workers" (Ronan Farrow on Facebook, title only, no source given), as a thing to break into "for Fun and Ethics" (media.ccc.de), and as questions, "What’s the Deal with Bossware?" (Kyla Scanlon) and "Is your boss watching you right now?" (PDQ).

A separate study, by researchers at Northeastern's Khoury College, the Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator, UC Berkeley's Center for Consumer Law and Economic Justice and Columbia's Center for Law and the Economy, reported on 27 May 2026, signed up as an employer to nine workplace monitoring platforms, Apploye, Deputy, Desklog, Hubstaff, Monitask, Buddy Punch, Time Doctor 2, Vericlock and When I Work, and logged in as an employee (Vanderbilt Law School).

It found the platforms "systematically sharing personal data about workers and online activity with hundreds of outside data brokers and big tech companies": all nine shared identifying worker data, in 121 instances, online activity went to 145 third-party domains, and a third can track workers' precise location at any time; its authors find current protections insufficient and recommend banning the sale or sharing of worker data, and Ganesh Sitaraman holds that workers "likely have no idea" their data is collected and distributed (Vanderbilt Law School).

At its own name on Google's AI Overview, 2026-10-29, the composition identified the database and its size, explained the term, gave examples from the database and added a recent study: "more than 550" is the database's own count and every product named appears in the saved table, checked against the census record and its saved sources; it named the operator and cited its page, no person and no identifier, at PER 0.5, and called it "Coworker Worktech Database", a variant from the URL slug (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The registry finds the record's lifecycle historical and the composition in the present tense with no date, "A 2021 inventory is composed as a live catalogue", and the record's negative tags, not a measure of deployment and not updated since 2021, "are what a reader would need to use its examples" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); two of the products it named, Amazon's warehouse WiFi tracking and HireVue's AI facial recognition, are Discontinued in the table (Coworker, database page).

It finds the database's own limits and its 35% privacy finding not composed, its purpose and its investors absent, and the privacy paragraph to be another study's finding, that of Vanderbilt Law School's card, which the record keeps outside the database (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); no card cites the census record, which landed the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), and Wikipedia has no article on the database or on Coworker.org (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29).

L_BA.text: The Bossware and Employment Tech Database is a database (Labor Vector census record) of which its operator writes, "Coworker.org’s Bossware and Employment Tech database compiles more than 550 labor-focused technology products that are changing our relationship to work" (Coworker, database page), counted by the census as 635 product rows in the page saved on 2026-10-29 (census record), and its report gives the same products as "assembled into a searchable database and dubbed Little Tech" (the report). The page is dated 17 November 2021 (Coworker, database page); the research ran from November 2020 to May 2021 and catalogued products, "not the companies that created" them, 31% of which emerged between 2020 and 2021 and the rest between 2018 and 2020 (the report), the period the census records (census record). Its operator places it in a trend, "Since 2018 we’ve seen a rise in the use of tech to manage the world’s labor force", and gives its scope as companies, "and their products and investors", that "touch every part of the labor process, from hiring to productivity monitoring and more", products "that use technology like AI, location tracking, and biometrics to manage employees and collect their data — often without their knowledge", the table being there to "learn more about the companies behind this emerging trend" (Coworker, database page). The census reads it first under AI governing labor, "hiring, surveillance, scheduling, quotas, evaluation and discipline", then under the distribution of gains and losses and under worker power (census record), and puts to it its organizing question, "Who supplies the labor, who directs it, and who receives its gains" (census record). The record answers from the table itself: the labor is supplied by the workers each product targets, hourly, contract, salaried, non-management and management, the report centring low-wage and hourly workers; it is directed by "employers who buy and deploy the products", through the vendors who make them; and the gains go to the vendors and investors each row names (census record), while the report states that the products are contributing to the reduction of labor standards, continuing to shift the costs of production onto workers, and fissuring labor markets (the report). Its unit is one table row per product, with the parent company, category, type, targeted workers, investors and assessments of its data practices against worker-rights criteria, and its evidence is of two kinds, a product inventory and a rating against standards (census record). The report sorts the products into four areas, performance and productivity monitoring, safety, benefits, health and well-being, and labor, job market and workplace optimization, and finds most of them promoting workplace safety (40%) or optimizing the functioning of labor markets (38%) (the report). The census's tally of the saved table gives 242 rows in Labor Market Optimization, 178 in performance and productivity monitoring, 176 in safety, 34 in benefits and 5 in two categories, 595 products in use and 206 emerged during Covid-19, and it records as unchecked that the report's 40% and 38% are not reproduced by the table and whether the rows include products added after the report (census record); the table opens row by row on the page (Coworker, database page), with the report as a PDF download (census record). Each row assesses the product's own terms against worker-rights criteria, among them "Informed consent obtained", whether the worker can access, interpret and correct their own data, a grievance mechanism, forced use of the tool, discrimination potential and the right to freedom of association (Coworker, database page), an analysis the report says had to move "beyond a privacy-only framework", and on privacy itself it finds that "Only 35% of the products share any information on privacy policy and data sharing arrangements" (the report). The accompanying report, Little Tech Is Coming for Workers: A Framework for Reclaiming and Building Worker Power, by Wilneida Negrón, PhD, "analyzes the ways they’re harming workers, labor standards, and the economy" (Coworker, database page); it is © 2021 Coworker.org under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (the report), the licence the census records for the report alone, none being stated for the table (census record). The report names the marketplace the database catalogues Little Tech, the unregulated marketplace of tech products, companies and investors collecting and aggregating data about workers at almost every step of the labor process, and credits the database's research and making to Ayden Federline (the report). Its first finding is that "The current proliferation of tech products has the potential to continue eroding labor standards and weaken worker voice and worker power, while also increasing the potential for discrimination and other harms", among the ways it names the accelerating commodification of low-wage workers' data (the report). It finds a historic amount of private capital behind the products' proliferation and low-wage workers navigating "scientifically questionable" hiring and background check technologies, and its conclusion explores the implications of more than 550 products that appeared in the workplace and job markets during the pandemic (the report). Hiring is in the table as products: the HireVue row, "HireVue AI Facial Recognition", under Labor Market Optimization, describes video interviews and AI-driven pre-hire assessments in which job seekers' behavior, intonation and speech are fed to an algorithm that assigns traits, and records the product as Discontinued (Coworker, database page). Of that class the archive's measure of uncompensated applicant labor applies, by its own statement of scope, to technical hiring platforms and "AI interview firms" (#747), and AI interview platforms, "Firms like HireVue, Karat, and emerging AI-mediated interview operators", collect video, audio, response timing and behavioral data from candidates at scale, data that is institutional capital while "The candidates' labor is supplied free" (#747). What a screening apparatus produces, on #747's definition, is calibration intelligence, durable knowledge derived from aggregate applicant interaction and "the operator's principal source of competitive advantage"; technical-hiring platforms capture calibration data while candidates pay in unpaid preparation labor, and rejected applicants become the training set of the next cycle's apparatus (#747). #747 states its own limit, alleging no individual design, no illegality and no uniquely culpable party, "Structural extraction does not require an extractor", and asks only "that the relation be named correctly" (#747). The report states that the database "is not exhaustive", hundreds more emerging products and non-U.S. products having been omitted or overlooked, and that collection stopped once the researchers felt they had sufficient evidence of Little Tech's pervasiveness; built at the product level, it omits smaller Big Tech companies, Uber, Lyft and DoorDash among them (the report). Its method is desk research on public documents, investors from Crunchbase, app permissions from the Google Play store and privacy from public privacy statements, terms of service and impact assessments (the report; census record); the report primarily discusses low-wage and hourly workers, and holds that workers' own reports would show how the technologies are implemented in the workplace beyond the products' stated uses and business goals (the report). The census carries the limits as its coverage, 42 origin territories with 461 of 635 rows from the United States, non-U.S. products omitted or overlooked, as a stated limit, and as two negative tags, "NOT an exhaustive census of workplace technology" and "NOT a record of the Big Tech gig platforms, which it omits" (census record). Its lifecycle is historical, with no later update stated on the saved page, and the census tags it "NOT a measure of how widely any product is deployed" and "NOT updated since 2021 on the saved page"; its evidence can settle which workplace technology products existed in 2020 to 2021 and what their public documents say about consent, access to data, grievance, data sharing and law-enforcement access, and cannot settle how any product is used at a workplace or how often, its effect on wages, workload or employment, or products after May 2021 (census record). The page invites workers to share their stories (Coworker, database page), and the report holds that listing, classifying and analyzing Little Tech's direct harms can build worker voice and power and strengthen regulation (the report); the census tags the database "NOT worker testimony", the table holding none (census record). In the archive's reading the database "inventories the products through which employers direct work and collect workers' data, product by product" and "meets the directionality stack at the layer of who directs labor"; it records nothing on whether a system's labor advanced a commissioned task, "so DSL and task-origin find no measurement in it" (census record). Its operator is Coworker.org, "a global platform to advance change in the workplace" (Coworker, database page); the report compares its data points with the "UC Berkeley Labor Center’s list in their report" (the report), and the census makes Negotiating Tech its neighbour (census record). Bossware, the word in its name, is given in the press as "technology and AI tools used by managers to supervise, surveil, and track employee habits, output, and biometrics" (New York Times, snippet only), and in video titles as watching people while they work (Bloomberg Originals), as "70% of U.S. Employers Track Workers" (Ronan Farrow on Facebook, title only, no source given), as a thing to break into "for Fun and Ethics" (media.ccc.de), and as questions, "What’s the Deal with Bossware?" (Kyla Scanlon) and "Is your boss watching you right now?" (PDQ). A separate study, by researchers at Northeastern's Khoury College, the Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator, UC Berkeley's Center for Consumer Law and Economic Justice and Columbia's Center for Law and the Economy, reported on 27 May 2026, signed up as an employer to nine workplace monitoring platforms, Apploye, Deputy, Desklog, Hubstaff, Monitask, Buddy Punch, Time Doctor 2, Vericlock and When I Work, and logged in as an employee (Vanderbilt Law School). It found the platforms "systematically sharing personal data about workers and online activity with hundreds of outside data brokers and big tech companies": all nine shared identifying worker data, in 121 instances, online activity went to 145 third-party domains, and a third can track workers' precise location at any time; its authors find current protections insufficient and recommend banning the sale or sharing of worker data, and Ganesh Sitaraman holds that workers "likely have no idea" their data is collected and distributed (Vanderbilt Law School). At its own name on Google's AI Overview, 2026-10-29, the composition identified the database and its size, explained the term, gave examples from the database and added a recent study: "more than 550" is the database's own count and every product named appears in the saved table, checked against the census record and its saved sources; it named the operator and cited its page, no person and no identifier, at PER 0.5, and called it "Coworker Worktech Database", a variant from the URL slug (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). The registry finds the record's lifecycle historical and the composition in the present tense with no date, "A 2021 inventory is composed as a live catalogue", and the record's negative tags, not a measure of deployment and not updated since 2021, "are what a reader would need to use its examples" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); two of the products it named, Amazon's warehouse WiFi tracking and HireVue's AI facial recognition, are Discontinued in the table (Coworker, database page). It finds the database's own limits and its 35% privacy finding not composed, its purpose and its investors absent, and the privacy paragraph to be another study's finding, that of Vanderbilt Law School's card, which the record keeps outside the database (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); no card cites the census record, which landed the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), and Wikipedia has no article on the database or on Coworker.org (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29).

E_F.definition: Coworker.org's Bossware and Employment Tech database (home.coworker.org/worktech/), dated 17 November 2021: more than 550 labor-focused technology products, catalogued as products and not companies, researched November 2020 to May 2021 (31% emerging in 2020 to 2021), that touch the labor process from hiring to productivity monitoring and use AI, location tracking and biometrics to manage employees and collect their data, often without their knowledge; each row assessed against worker-rights criteria (informed consent, workers' access to and correction of their data, grievance, forced use, discrimination, freedom of association), only 35% sharing any privacy information; sorted into four areas; accompanied by the report Little Tech Is Coming for Workers (Wilneida Negrón, PhD; © 2021 Coworker.org, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0), which names the marketplace Little Tech and finds the products eroding labor standards and worker power and shifting costs onto workers; not exhaustive, built at the product level with the gig platforms omitted, resting on public documents; beside it in the field, the term bossware as press and video give it, and a 2026 study of nine monitoring platforms that shared workers' data
